baer-heitev/1:_: He borrowed. And Kenesset HaGedolah wrote that there are places that practiced forbidding l'chatchila to borrow before Pesach and repay after Pesach; and see siman 448 s.k. 11, end of his words.
baer-heitev/2:_: He should tell him. And b'dieved, even if he did not tell him and the non-Jew brought him [payment] after Pesach it is permitted, for the Jew did not acquire it on Pesach (Bach, Magen Avraham). And Kaf HaChayyim wrote that l'chatchila it is good to stipulate thus; and if he stipulated thus, even if the non-Jew later gives him chametz over which Passover passed, it is also permitted; and if he did not stipulate with him thus, if the non-Jew gives him afterwards flour or money or chametz made after Pesach it is permitted. And the same law applies to one who purchases the priests' allotment who give them fixed bread every week — see Taz (who was inclined to be stringent and requires a condition, and concluded that if they did not stipulate at first the transaction is voided and he stipulates — see siman 245 above). And one should not be stringent in these laws, for in any event a Jew does not acquire without pulling according to most poskim (Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/3:_: Afterwards. And the Acharonim agreed to practice that he sell the oven to the non-Jew on Pesach and take the money that comes for his share (Kaf HaChayyim, end of his words). Nevertheless, on a Shabbat within Pesach it does not help through what he says "take yours" as on other Shabbats of the year, as written siman 245, unless they stipulated at the beginning of the partnership (end of his words). And Magen Avraham wrote: and on the four days that are yom tov, in any event it is forbidden to tell him "take yours" (end of his words); and Kaf HaChayyim disagrees with him (end of his words).
baer-heitev/4:א: To receive. Since the oven belongs to the Jew; and do not say for seif 3 that there it is a partnership oven (Taz s.k. 3); and see in Kenesset HaGedolah.
baer-heitev/4:ב: To benefit. For chametz does not take its value, as written siman 443; but if he received the loaves it is forbidden to benefit from them, for he acquired them on Pesach as wage for his oven, since their custom is always to give loaves — and if so it is chametz of a Jew over which Passover passed (Magen Avraham).
baer-heitev/5:א: Matzah. Taz challenged this law and left it as requiring further study; and Kaf HaChayyim reconciled and answered (end of his words) (for he concluded: nevertheless he should say that he bake matzah in it).
baer-heitev/5:ב: To dwell. The agreement of Rishonim and Acharonim: even though he rented it to him unstipulated to dwell in it, this comes only to exclude where he rented it explicitly for chametz — when he rented it during Pesach or on erev Pesach (from several hours and upward) (end of his words, Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/6:א: Chametz. And if he is hired by him for a year he should not eat in his house because of suspicion (Agudah).
baer-heitev/6:ב: And eat. If he knows he will eat chametz (Magen Avraham). And the meaning of the language of the Gemara implies that even with a mere concern it is forbidden (Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/6:ג: They permit. And yes, this is the main ruling (Magen Avraham). But Bach, Kenesset HaGedolah, and Kaf HaChayyim ruled like the first opinion to be stringent.
baer-heitev/6:ד: Dinar. Specifically when the dinar is still in existence in the shopkeeper's hand at the time he eats. And if he did not give him the dinar beforehand, it is permitted to say: give the workers chametz and I will pay — and if so, one who has a child who needs to drink chametz may tell a non-Jew: give him to drink chametz and I will pay; but he should not take the chametz in his hand. And Kaf HaChayyim wrote that he should not say "and I will pay" (Bach). And for a sick person in danger, everything is permitted (Magen Avraham, end of his words); and see Magen Avraham siman 443 and responsum Nishmat Shabbat siman 14; and see responsum Bach siman 43. Nevertheless it is good to make a partition of ten [tefachim] to separate so that he not come to eat from it (Kaf HaChayyim, end of his words).
baer-heitev/6:ה: Of the non-Jew. For there is no agency for a non-Jew, and the Jew ends up buying them; and further there is concern lest he eat from it; and further it appears he wants its continued existence (Magen Avraham).
baer-heitev/7:א: Utensils. The reason he wants its continued existence is that the chametz remain and be sustained inside — for if he removes the chametz from the pot while it is still on the fire the vessel may crack at the fire and then he benefits from chametz; but in an oven this does not apply. And further, since the vessel itself is forbidden in benefit because the pot absorbed chametz, it is forbidden to rent it l'chatchila; but an oven, when one bakes in it, is already fired and does not absorb chametz (Magen Avraham). Taz wrote: but three or four weeks before Pesach it is permitted in every case — see there.
baer-heitev/7:ב: Chametz. The agreement of Acharonim: here it deals with one who rented unstipulated and did not specify to bring chametz on it (end of his words). Bach wrote what is practiced in Poland: Jews rent an estate from the lord that has cauldrons and mills; they take a measure from every wage of beer cooked in cauldrons, and likewise take a measure of malt from everyone who grinds malt — if the Jew is obligated to repair the cauldrons and mills when they break, then they are in the Jew's possession and it is forbidden to receive even money as his wage, since their custom is to give chametz — it is like benefiting from chametz money and is forbidden. And if he has authority and power to prevent them from cooking at all, he is obligated to prevent them, for this is wanting its continued existence; and through sale it is permitted — that is, he sell before Pesach to a non-Jew all the measures that will come from this week and take the money, and even though the non-Jew gives him the measures afterwards it is permitted. And if the Jew need not repair the cauldrons and mills, it suffices to stipulate before Pesach as in seif 2. And if he has no one with whom to stipulate, it is like b'dieved and permitted without a condition (end of his words); and see Taz and Magen Avraham.
baer-heitev/7:ג: Benefit. Such as to place cold in it temporarily on dry [food], or something moist that is not an eating matter, such as washing — and specifically if it is temporary so we are not concerned he will use it for another use (Kaf HaChayyim). And Rashal forbids only washing the head. And see responsum Sha'agat Aryeh siman 66 regarding a Jew who was hired for a year to guard wine — whether it is permitted to guard and receive money for the wage on Pesach; see there.
beer-hagolah/1:_: Tur in the name of Rashi, and the rest of the poskim from what is in Beit Rabbi Yannai 61b
beer-hagolah/2:_: Tur in the name of Avi HaEzri
beer-hagolah/3:_: Tur in the name of responsum of Rashi:
beer-hagolah/4:א: Tur in the name of Rashba, and there it is explicit that they brought it to him after Pesach
beer-hagolah/4:ב: there; and see above at the end of siman 443
beer-hagolah/5:_: there from Mishnah at the beginning of chapter 5 of Avodah Zarah
beer-hagolah/6:א: Tur and Mordechai in chapter 2 of Pesachim
beer-hagolah/6:ב: from what is in Avodah Zarah 63
beer-hagolah/7:א: Tur, because he wants the existence of the prohibition so the vessel will not crack
beer-hagolah/7:ב: Tur in the name of Tosafot
machatzit-hashekel/1:א: (s.k. 1) He must [repay] etc. — and even though l'chatchila etc.; meaning: we hold chametz does not take its value and its substitutes are permitted, as written siman 443 — nevertheless l'chatchila it is forbidden etc.
machatzit-hashekel/1:ב: The first is not in existence etc. — and therefore Kaf HaChayyim wrote that even if he pays him on Pesach something that is not chametz it is permitted; and so too from the words of Tosafot in Avodah Zarah, from which we learn the law here: they say in the beginning of the chapter of workers in Beit Rabbi Yannai — the poor borrow shevi'it produce in shevi'it and repay in the eighth year with eighth-year produce. Tosafot wrote there the reason: since at the time of repayment the shevi'it produce is not in existence they are not shevi'it substitutes; all the more so with chametz that does not take its value. Tosafot wrote there that likewise if they repaid them in shevi'it with other produce that is not shevi'it, if they already ate what they borrowed from the poor it is permitted; and so it appears from the words of the Rosh — all the more so with chametz. Kenesset HaGedolah wrote there are places that practiced etc., and Kaf HaChayyim wrote in his name because of interest prohibition they touched on it, like se'ah bese'ah which is forbidden — and so too Darkei Moshe; not because of chametz prohibition. Therefore according to what Rama wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 462 that we practice leniency with loaves because people are not particular about such a small matter — the custom Kenesset HaGedolah wrote does not apply.
machatzit-hashekel/2:_: (s.k. 2) He should say etc. — and a Jew who bought the priests' allotment etc. — permitted to take etc.; from this wording it implies that even l'chatchila he need not stipulate before Pesach; and so the Magen Avraham inferred from this wording. Therefore it must be said the priests' allotment is more lenient than one who receives loaves with interest — and that is not so; on the contrary the priests' allotment has reason to be more stringent, as Taz wrote s.k. 1. Rather, according to Mordechai, as the Magen Avraham understood (see chapter 8): he holds regarding the priests' allotment that one need not stipulate before Pesach — likewise regarding receiving loaves with interest he holds one need not stipulate, as the Magen Avraham wrote (end of his words); but we do not hold like him, and for us, since one must stipulate with interest-loaves, all the more so with the priests' allotment. Magen Avraham understood Mordechai's wording regarding the priests' allotment to teach that we are lenient there as with interest-loaves; and regarding a condition he relied on Magen Avraham himself, for we know it is no better than interest-loaves.
machatzit-hashekel/3:א: (s.k. 3) He says etc. — but here, when he takes etc.; meaning: here there is no prohibition, for it does not appear as trouble for the Jew — what of it if he troubles for the Jew, for it deals with chol hamoed as Magen Avraham wrote in that s.k. 7; and even though on chol hamoed melacha not needed for the festival is forbidden, nevertheless it is not so severe and there is no marit ayin here; the prohibition is only from receiving chametz on Pesach as his wage — therefore by taking the money first it is permitted, for then he sells the chametz before Pesach and then it is permitted to sell it, as explained below.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ב: For Rambam and the Rosh: the Rosh's view regarding a Jew and a non-Jew who were partners in trees — even if they did not stipulate before partnering, the Jew may tell the non-Jew: take for yourself three years of orlah and I will take correspondingly three other years; for what should we be concerned — if because of marit ayin when the non-Jew works the orlah years it appears he is the Jew's agent? What of it — the Jew himself may work the tree in orlah years. And if because the Jew takes three years of fruit against three years of orlah fruit — that would be orlah substitutes. They say: such is the custom — whoever works the tree eats its fruit; and since the non-Jew passes the orlah years the fruit is all the non-Jew's, and the three years the Jew works the fruit is all his — there are no orlah substitutes at all. Therefore likewise here regarding chametz — this is Mordechai's view like the Rosh there; but Rambam holds that even for orlah one must stipulate specifically before they partnered, but afterwards saying "take yours" does not help — even though the non-Jew works alone in orlah years and the Jew alone in the other three years, nevertheless it is orlah substitutes. The same applies — one should forbid chametz here; and Hagahot Maimoniyot holds like Rambam. Therefore he holds one must take the money first, and that suffices, as written afterwards.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ג: Only that he sells the chametz to the non-Jew etc. — meaning: if he sells chametz to the non-Jew before Pesach — even though there is reason to permit, for then the chametz is still permitted to eat, all the more so to sell — nevertheless Magen Avraham holds this reason does not help: specifically to benefit and to sell chametz he already acquired is permitted, but here he sells and benefits from chametz that will be acquired on Pesach at the time of prohibition — that is benefiting on Pesach from issurei hana'ah; and so Bach wrote (end of his words). Therefore Magen Avraham wrote we require selling him the oven; and Hagahot Maimoniyot's view is that we require taking money first. It must be said that saying "take yours on Pesach" does not help — through this we say he sells him the oven since the oven already belongs to the Jew. And why taking money first helps — I do not know a clear reason; possibly: since chametz substitutes are b'dieved permitted but l'chatchila forbidden to receive substitutes, and since the substitute-buyer, i.e. the money, is before Pesach, before he acquired chametz, it is permitted even l'chatchila; and Magen Avraham for the practical law is stringent that we require sale of the oven and also taking money before Pesach.
machatzit-hashekel/3:ד: And on the four days that are yom tov etc. — and Kaf HaChayyim wondered: on yom tov burning is permitted — what of it if they say the non-Jew acts as the Jew's agent; they forbade only on Shabbat in siman 245. And he answered well in Sefer Ateret Roshei: likewise on yom tov it is forbidden since he bakes chametz in it for the non-Jew's need.
machatzit-hashekel/5:_: (s.k. 5) One is not concerned etc. — as explained clearly above; and Beit Yosef strained on this (end of his words). Meaning: Tur brought this law in the name of Rashba, and Rashba brings proof from what we learn in Avodah Zarah at the beginning of the chapter of the hirer: he hired him to do another work with him, even though he told him pass me barrels of yayin nesech from place to place — permitted. The Magen Avraham challenged: there is no proof, for payment for passing those barrels is not on passing them but on the work he hired him to do. Therefore the Magen Avraham wrote Rashba explains that mishnah another way — the simple understood way; but Magen Avraham holds Rashba also explains the mishnah as above, and nevertheless brings proof properly: wherever even if the forbidden thing were not done he would have to give wages — even though that forbidden thing was done, the wage is permitted. If so, here too the wage is permitted: for even if the non-Jew did not bake at all he would have to give oven-rent — therefore even if he baked chametz in it the wage is permitted. Nevertheless l'chatchila he must say he bake matzah, for if not, since it is known his custom is to bake chametz in it, it is as if he rented it for baking chametz — and renting is forbidden.
machatzit-hashekel/6:_: (s.k. 6) To dwell etc. — and specifically etc. during Pesach or erev Pesach; and in Peri Chadash it implies specifically before thirty days; and so at the beginning of Agur's words; and Peri Chadash wrote that lending for free or borrowing is permitted (end of his words).
magen-avraham/1:_: He must repay him. And even though l'chatchila it is forbidden to receive chametz substitutes here, since when he gives him this loaf the first is not in existence they are not chametz substitutes (end of his words, siman 443); and Kenesset HaGedolah wrote there are places that practiced forbidding l'chatchila to borrow before Pesach and repay after Pesach.
magen-avraham/2:_: He should tell him etc. And b'dieved, even if he did not tell him and he brought him after Pesach it is permitted, for the Jew did not acquire it on Pesach (Bach). And a Jew who bought the priests' allotment who give them bread — permitted to take after Pesach what they withheld from him on Pesach, for chametz over which Passover passed is not forbidden except from a fine, and it appears we do not fine him (Hagahot Maimoniyot and Mordechai).
magen-avraham/3:_: He tells the non-Jew etc. Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot that it is permitted to stipulate before Pesach and take money etc.; and do not say regarding a Jew and non-Jew who have a field in partnership that it is forbidden to say "take yours for Shabbat and mine for weekday" as siman 245 — there all the trouble is shared and it appears as trouble for the Jew; but here, when he takes money first, it is permitted (end of Hagahot Maimoniyot). But Mordechai wrote as here, that he need not take money. It appears they dispute the dispute of Rambam and Rosh in Yoreh De'ah siman 294 seif 13 regarding orlah (end of his words); if so, it requires further study on the Magen Avraham, since he ruled there it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew "take your share in orlah years and I afterwards" — that is orlah substitutes, and here too it should be forbidden. One may say: here the Jew never acquired chametz — he only sells the oven to the non-Jew on Pesach and the non-Jew can bake matzah in it; not so there where he acquired trees. Nevertheless one should practice selling the oven to the non-Jew on Pesach and taking money first as Hagahot Maimoniyot wrote, and so Bach; and on the four days that are yom tov it is in any event forbidden to say "take yours" etc. as siman 245.
magen-avraham/4:_: Permitted to benefit. For chametz does not take its value, as siman 443; but if he received loaves it is forbidden to benefit from them, for he acquired them on Pesach as wage for his oven, since their custom is always to give loaves — and if so it is chametz of a Jew over which Passover passed.
magen-avraham/5:א: One is not concerned about him. And even though if he hired him to do another work and afterwards did yayin nesech with him his wage is forbidden — there, if he did nothing with him he would not pay wages and he would take yayin nesech wage; but here, since he rented his oven for one week, even if the non-Jew did not bake at all he would have to pay — he does not take chametz wage, therefore permitted. Nevertheless l'chatchila he must say they bake matzah in it, as explained clearly; and Beit Yosef strained on this (end of his words).
magen-avraham/5:ב: To dwell in it. It implies it is forbidden to rent to him for chametz, for he profits from issurei hana'ah (and so Taz); and specifically when he rented during Pesach or erev Pesach (Agur).
magen-avraham/6:א: That he acquire chametz. And if he is hired by him for a year he should not eat in his house because of suspicion (Agudah).
magen-avraham/6:ב: Go and eat. And specifically if he told him go and eat chametz, or he knows certainly he will eat chametz.
magen-avraham/6:ג: Unless he gave beforehand etc. And so is the main ruling; and specifically when the dinar is still in existence in the shopkeeper's hand when he eats, as Yoreh De'ah siman 332 seif 4; and if he did not give dinar beforehand, permitted to say: give the workers chametz and I will pay. If so, one who has a child who needs to drink chametz may tell a non-Jew: give him to drink chametz and I will pay (and see siman 443); and this is not benefit in what we built that he drinks chametz, as Yoreh De'ah siman 221 seif 4 (end of his words); and further workers' sustenance is on him and nevertheless permitted as Mordechai wrote (end of his words); but he should not take chametz in his hand (and siman 326 seif 1 in the gloss); as siman 446 seif 3; and for a sick person in danger everything is permitted.
magen-avraham/6:ד: And forbidden to buy. For there is no agency for a non-Jew and the Jew ends up buying them; and further there is concern lest he eat from it (Rivash, Beit Yosef); and further it appears forbidden because he wants its continued existence, as Yoreh De'ah siman 332 seif 4, end of his words; and so Tosafot in Pesachim 102b — what the non-Jew holds as a favor is considered wage unless it is not in the non-Jew's presence (end of his words); and from their words it implies: if the non-Jew's animal was laden with chametz it is forbidden to unload except not in the non-Jew's presence; but for the first version it is permitted since there is pain for the animal on a Torah level and he does not intend the non-Jew hold a favor for him — it is not possible and not intended, and permitted; and so Choshen Mishpat siman 272 in Tur (end of his words).
magen-avraham/7:א: Forbidden to rent etc. Because he wants its continued existence through something else so the vessel not crack (Tur). It appears the reason is he wants the chametz remain and be sustained inside — if he removes chametz from the pot while on the fire the vessel cracks at the fire and then he benefits from chametz; but in an oven this does not apply, unlike Beit Yosef. And further, since the vessel itself is forbidden in benefit, forbidden to rent l'chatchila (Tur) — meaning the pot absorbed chametz; but an oven when one bakes in it is already fired and does not absorb chametz. It is difficult — it should be forbidden because of profiting from issurei hana'ah as seif 4; it must be said specifically there they give chametz itself as oven-payment, for such was their custom — those monies are also chametz money; but for utensils the main wage is money, only chametz caused him benefit — they did not be stringent to forbid; the same for a donkey. Nevertheless it appears to forbid even for a donkey (Bach); and his words require further study, for Rashba brings proof from yayin nesech that renting is forbidden and there the main rental is money; and one may challenge: a house too — main rental is money and nevertheless forbidden as seif 5 in the gloss. Therefore it appears all these deal when he rents unstipulated only knowing the non-Jew will use it (for chametz); therefore for an oven it is forbidden, since he rents it for baking and unstipulated baking is chametz — he profits from issurei hana'ah, therefore he must say to bake matzah; but for utensils and donkey they do not presume chametz, therefore unstipulated permitted to rent for cooking; forbidden for utensils for another reason as above; for donkey permitted. And what Rama wrote regarding a house rented to dwell — when rented unstipulated as above; and in Beit Yosef siman 440 in the name of Rashba it implies specifically for a house where he sits and guards it is forbidden.
magen-avraham/7:ב: And some permit etc. At first glance it requires further study what this has to do here; but Darkei Moshe wrote: according to Tur who forbids renting because the vessel itself absorbed chametz — all the more forbidden to heat in it for his own benefit. Nevertheless the custom is permitted, and so Tosafot (end of his words); and it requires further study, for Mordechai permitted a chicken in which wheat was found to sell to a non-Jew since he has no benefit from the chametz — and on this Mordechai brings proof that heating water in chametz vessels is permitted since one does not benefit from the absorption etc. (end of his words); and we hold a dish in which chametz was found — everything is forbidden in benefit, as siman 447 (and the reason — see siman 442 seif 2); and forbidden to sell to a non-Jew — all the more forbidden to wash in it; and in Tosafot they permitted only to put something dry inside — Tur does not dispute, for he ruled Yoreh De'ah siman 94 that a pot absorbed meat in milk may have fruit or cold placed in it; and Or Zarua wrote everywhere water permitted in benefit may be sold to a non-Jew — if so, since here permitted to wash, we may say likewise a dish cooked in chametz utensils may be sold to a non-Jew. In Ma'agalei Tzedek it is written these utensils are not eating utensils but specifically for washing and laundering — even though they absorbed chametz, by law they need not be hidden from sight like other vessels (Arukh, Tanakh) — nevertheless it must be that now they are not used at all on Pesach (end of his words). Nevertheless even according to Maharitz it appears since they absorbed somewhat and are not b'ein, they are not forbidden in benefit; if so, if a dish was cooked in them it may be sold to a non-Jew; and see Taz chapter 80 who ruled regarding a pot absorbed meat in milk that it is permitted to heat water to wash the head, and nevertheless forbidden to sell to a non-Jew; it must be said a food item — when the non-Jew eats and enjoys it, it is as if the Jew benefits, for his benefit is from the non-Jew, as siman 448; but to wash the head with it is permitted since he does not benefit from chametz inside; and further it is not the usual manner of their benefit, as siman 466. In Yeshuot Yaakov on Chullin he wrote: specifically hot water to wash the head — custom is lenient; but what is fit for food and drink is forbidden (end of his words); if so, here too forbidden to sell to a non-Jew. Bach wrote: those who rent from the lord cauldrons and mills take a measure of chametz from every beer wage cooked in cauldrons — if the Jew must repair cauldrons and mills when broken, they are in the Jew's possession and forbidden to receive even money as wage, since their custom is to give chametz — like benefiting from chametz money; and if he can prevent them from cooking he must, for wanting its continued existence; and through sale permitted — sell before Pesach to a non-Jew all measures from this week and take money, even though the non-Jew gives measures afterwards, as siman 448 seif 3 (and it appears he should also sell the cauldrons to the non-Jew). If the Jew need not repair cauldrons and mills — like one who bought the priests' allotment as seif 2; it suffices to stipulate before Pesach; if he has no one to stipulate with, b'dieved permitted without condition (end of his words). It appears the priests' allotment is not rental but a mere tax — if they do not give today they give tomorrow; but here he gives wage for mills and cauldrons and the non-Jew separates it — it is actual money like an oven; even money forbidden as wage, profiting from issurei hana'ah; and even if he need not repair, they are his for the hour — rental is daily, not sale; what does the lord care if the Jew leaves them empty or lets his cook grind — therefore no permission except selling mills and cauldrons before Pesach (end of his words, siman 443 gloss); it must deal when the Jew does not rent the mills themselves but rents the lord's allotment from the mills, i.e. the measures; nevertheless it appears unlike the priests' allotment: immediately when they grind chametz and separate the measure and leave it in the mill the Jew acquired his measure — therefore he may sell to a non-Jew or command the grinders not to separate measures on Pesach but write the non-Jew ground on Pesach and collect after Pesach, as above.
mechaber/1:main: The law of a Jew and a non-Jew who have a partnership. Contains 7 seifim. A Jew who borrowed a loaf from his fellow Jew before Pesach must repay it after Pesach; and there is a matter of theft if he does not repay it.
mechaber/2:main: A Jew who receives from a non-Jew interest-loaves every week — he should tell him before Pesach to give him during the week of Pesach flour or money; and since he stipulated thus with him, even though after Pesach he gives him chametz loaves in place of the flour and money, it is permitted.
mechaber/3:main: A Jew and a non-Jew who have an oven in partnership — he tells the non-Jew before Pesach: take yours for Pesach, and I will take mine afterwards.
mechaber/4:main: A Jew who had an oven and a non-Jew baked chametz in it on Pesach — even money is forbidden to receive as his wage, for it would be profiting from issurei hana'ah; and if he already received the money, it is permitted to benefit from it.
mechaber/5:main: There are those who permit renting his oven to a non-Jew on condition that he bake matzah in it; and if he bakes chametz in it, one is not concerned about it. {Rama: And likewise it is permitted to rent him a house to dwell in, even though he may later bring chametz into it. (Agur)}
mechaber/6:main: One may say to a worker on Pesach: take this dinar and buy and eat, even though he knows he will acquire chametz; but he should not tell him: go and eat and I will pay. There are those who permit even this, except if he gave the dinar beforehand or handed it over. {Rama: And it is forbidden to buy chametz for a non-Jew on Pesach, even with the non-Jew's money. (Rivash siman 41)}
mechaber/7:main: It is forbidden to rent utensils to a non-Jew on Pesach so that he cook chametz in them; but one may rent him a donkey to bring chametz on it. {Rama: And some permit heating water in chametz utensils and washing in them, and likewise other needs of benefit from chametz utensils; and such is the custom. (Tosafot perek Ein Ma'amidin; Mordechai perek Kol Sha'ah)}
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) Before Pesach he must repay him — meaning even if he borrowed this loaf on erev Pesach near the time of burning: if he had not borrowed it, he would have had to burn it, and if he did not burn it it would be forbidden in benefit — nevertheless he must return another loaf after Pesach, for in any event he borrowed at a permitted time when the chametz was full property still before burning time. Acharonim wrote: even if the Jew transgressed and borrowed and kept the chametz until after Pesach and it became forbidden, nevertheless he must pay and we do not say the lender cannot receive its value because of chametz substitutes as above siman 443, for this is not chametz substitutes — since he borrowed the loaf it is his and the lender has only monetary claim. A Jew who lent chametz to a non-Jew before Pesach and repaid chametz like it after Pesach — since he does not return the first chametz in its existence it is permitted [so Shelah in the name of Riaz]; and from his words it implies if he returns that chametz it is forbidden. Peri Chadash disagrees — it is not called chametz over which Passover passed, for until now it belonged to the non-Jew; since he lent it, it stood in his possession and it is chametz of a non-Jew over which Passover passed, permitted even for eating. In practice one should be stringent like the first opinion — it appears as chametz of a Jew over which Passover passed since he returned that chametz itself.
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (2) If he does not repay him — and because of concern for interest, for it is forbidden to lend se'ah bese'ah — there is no such concern with loaves because the difference is a small matter according to most, and people are not particular about this (Acharonim).
mishnah-berurah/2:א: (3) He should tell him before — the reason: since he is obligated to give him a loaf every week, when the non-Jew designates the loaf on Pesach for the Jew it is as if he already acquired it and as if Passover passed on the Jew's chametz — therefore he must stipulate that for the week of Pesach he does not want loaves but their flour or equivalent money [or that he give loaves baked after Pesach]; if so, even if the non-Jew prepared loaves on Pesach we are not concerned, for they are not subjugated to the Jew at all and are entirely in the non-Jew's possession for now.
mishnah-berurah/2:ב: (4) Chametz loaves — meaning even those prepared for him on Pesach; and Acharonim agreed all this is l'chatchila, but b'dieved even if he did not stipulate at all it is permitted to receive loaves after Pesach for the week of Pesach; and even though he designated them for the Jew on Pesach — all this did not come into the Jew's possession, he did not acquire them, and he has only a monetary debt of loaves, not those bodies themselves, and they still belong to the non-Jew all Pesach days.
mishnah-berurah/3:א: (5) He tells the non-Jew before Pesach etc. — and if he did not say, forbidden to receive after Pesach for his share even money, as explained below.
mishnah-berurah/3:ב: (6) And I will take afterwards — some Acharonim wrote: specifically when he says "and I will take afterwards money against the loaf you took" — that is considered saying he does not want to rent his oven for work on Pesach except for money; or it deals when he says "take for yourself this week of Pesach the oven whether there is [bread] in it or not and I will take the week before or after what happens to me" — that is permitted, for they divide time and have no claim on each other. But when he says "take the loaves that will be on Pesach and I will take this amount afterwards" — then he wants the loaves in the oven [for if nothing is baked on Pesach in his oven the non-Jew will not give him after Pesach] and he acquires the oven for the Jew, only exchanging with the non-Jew partner; if so he benefits from his chametz on Pesach under his share in those loaves — the non-Jew gives him his share of loaves in the week after Pesach and it is forbidden. Some forbid even when he says "and I will take afterwards money against the loaves you took" — nevertheless he benefits from the value of his chametz on Pesach. Acharonim agreed that in practice one should practice selling the oven to the non-Jew for the week of Pesach so it is entirely in his possession, set a price for this, and take money from him first before Pesach — with this there is no prohibition from what occurs that Shabbat and yom tov week while it is absorbed.
mishnah-berurah/4:א: (7) And a non-Jew baked in it etc. — and it implies even without the owner's knowledge; and so Acharonim.
mishnah-berurah/4:ב: (8) Even money — all the more loaves from those who baked on Pesach; forbidden to receive, even after Pesach.
mishnah-berurah/4:ג: (9) For it is profiting etc. — forbidden l'chatchila d'rabbanan from all issurei hana'ah, even if he gives money before or after Pesach; and unlike seif 3 where the oven was partners' and when they divide at the time it was entirely the non-Jew's oven.
mishnah-berurah/4:ד: (10) Permitted to benefit from them — profiting from issurei hana'ah is not forbidden b'dieved anywhere where it is not the body of chametz or its substitute, only money came through chametz as cause — they were not stringent except for yayin nesech because of idolatry stringency. All this if he received money; but if they gave him loaves baked in his oven, forbidden to benefit, for he already acquired them on Pesach as oven-wage if their custom is always to give loaves — it is chametz of a Jew over which Passover passed.
mishnah-berurah/5:א: (11) To rent his oven to a non-Jew on condition etc. — this is not profiting from issurei hana'ah forbidden l'chatchila, since even if the non-Jew baked nothing he would have to pay the Jew his wage, for he rented for a set time — the Jew does not profit from what the non-Jew bakes chametz. Nevertheless l'chatchila he must tell him to bake matzah, for otherwise since it is known his custom is to bake chametz it is as if he rented for baking chametz, which is forbidden.
mishnah-berurah/5:ב: (12) A house to dwell in — meaning even though he rented unstipulated to dwell, it comes only to exclude renting explicitly for chametz, and because he profits from issurei hana'ah; and from Acharonim' words it seems we do not forbid profiting from issurei hana'ah except when its prohibition time arrived, such as on Pesach or erev Pesach; but before, not forbidden even l'chatchila. Some are stringent even within thirty days before Pesach.
mishnah-berurah/6:א: (13) To a worker — even though his sustenance is on him, since he did not tell him to acquire chametz.
mishnah-berurah/6:ב: (14) Even though he knows he will acquire etc. — and if he is hired for a year he should not eat in his house because of suspicion (Agudah).
mishnah-berurah/6:ג: (15) Chametz — but he should not tell him: take this dinar and buy chametz from the shopkeeper and eat, even if he is a non-Jew of the world whose sustenance is not on him — since the Jew himself is forbidden to buy chametz on Pesach, forbidden to tell a non-Jew to buy it; even though the non-Jew buys for himself and not for the Jew, since the Jew gives him a dinar and tells him to buy chametz with it and the non-Jew buys by his word, it appears as his agent. Permitted to tell him: buy chametz for yourself with your dinar and eat.
mishnah-berurah/6:ד: (16) Go and eat etc. — and specifically if he told him go and eat chametz, or at least he knows certainly he will eat chametz. The reason: since the shopkeeper gives the worker on credit that the master will pay, the shopkeeper is his agent and it is as if he feeds him chametz by hand; and since his sustenance is on him, he benefits from the chametz he feeds him.
mishnah-berurah/6:ה: (17) And some permit etc. — since he has not yet given money to the shopkeeper, what the shopkeeper gives his worker is not considered his chametz but a mere debt — he became obligated to the non-Jew for guaranteeing him. For practical law the main view is this; nevertheless l'chatchila proper to be concerned for the first view regarding his worker and maidservant whose sustenance is on him — not to tell him to go buy on credit but to give cash and he buys what he wants.
mishnah-berurah/6:ו: (18) Also in this — according to this view permitted also to tell the shopkeeper: give workers chametz and I will pay, for the same reason. Regarding a child who must eat and drink chametz — he should bring him to a non-Jew's house and ask the non-Jew to feed chametz to the child [but beware they not take it in hand, for he acquires it]; and if the non-Jew does not want to give free, he may promise to pay afterwards, for permitted by essential law as above; but he should not give money beforehand or when giving to eat, for he buys chametz thereby and forbidden to all; and if impossible to carry out and the non-Jew must bring chametz to the Jew's house and feed there, he may tell the non-Jew to gather leftover chametz and take to his house, and when needing to eat again return and bring and feed; and if no non-Jew each time, there is room to be lenient that the non-Jew leave chametz in the house for several times and explicitly say he does not want to acquire the chametz [otherwise he acquires for him], as above siman 448; and command a minor to feed the child — but he himself should not feed: forbidden l'chatchila to touch, as siman 446; and further because of acquisition concern. If he can hide chametz where sold chametz is kept, hide there and bring the child to eat; if not, make a ten-[tefach] partition before chametz, or at least cover with a vessel; all this if the child is not endangered — if danger, no need to be exact to hurry feeding, as siman 328.
mishnah-berurah/6:ז: (19) Unless he gave dinar beforehand — to the shopkeeper and commanded him to give sustenance to his worker when he comes — then it is like feeding chametz by hand, for the shopkeeper is the master's agent; with this forbidden even if he does not know certainly he will buy chametz; and see Yoreh De'ah siman 332 seif 4 who wrote: even giving dinar beforehand is not forbidden unless he said this dinar is in your hand until you give my worker; but if he permitted him to spend now, permitted — for when he gives the worker there is no dinar acquiring for the master. Many Acharonim disputed and agreed forbidden in all cases. Know: giving dinar beforehand is not precise — likewise if he gave dinar when the shopkeeper gave chametz to his worker, also forbidden; and this comes only to exclude if he paid afterwards.
mishnah-berurah/6:ח: (20) Or he lifted and gave by hand — meaning the master himself took chametz from the non-Jew shopkeeper for his worker and gave him; with this, even if he gave no money at all, nevertheless forbidden, for he acquired chametz by pulling from the non-Jew.
mishnah-berurah/6:ט: (21) And forbidden to buy etc. — there is concern lest he eat from it; and further he wants the chametz's continued existence; and further there is no agency for a non-Jew and the Jew ends up buying them and transgresses bal yera'eh; and even if he does not pull chametz from the seller's domain but only gives money on Pesach, also forbidden — for some say a Jew acquires movable property from a non-Jew with money alone.
mishnah-berurah/6:י: (22) Even with his money etc. — nevertheless if he did not intend to buy for himself and also took no liability, there is room to be lenient for eating and benefit after Pesach, as Peri Megadim wrote; and see Sha'arei Teshuvah.
mishnah-berurah/6:כ: (23) Of the non-Jew — likewise forbidden to tell a non-Jew on chol hamoed Pesach to buy chametz for him, even if he does not draw chametz into the Jew's house — some poskim hold there is agency for a non-Jew stringently; b'dieved if he bought and did not draw to his domain, no prohibition after Pesach [from Chiddushei R' Akiva Eiger, end of his words]. Peri Megadim wrote regarding a non-Jew buying grain from a non-Jew with some souring — permitted for a Jew to be broker between them, for he does not pay for the sour part. If the non-Jew's animal was laden with chametz, permitted to unload where there is pain for the animal on a Torah level — even though the non-Jew holds a favor for this [and this is generally wanting continued existence of chametz so he holds a favor] — since the Jew does not intend he hold a favor, permitted.
mishnah-berurah/7:א: (24) So that he cook chametz in them — because he wants the chametz's continued existence [that if he pours chametz from the pot while on the fire the vessel may crack] — and behold it is like benefiting from chametz.
mishnah-berurah/7:ב: (25) But one may rent him a donkey — for he does not care if the chametz is lost. Acharonim challenged: why forbid both utensils and donkey because of profiting from issurei hana'ah forbidden l'chatchila as previous seifim; they conclude this law is for the view that profiting from issurei hana'ah is forbidden only for idolatry and the like; but according to what we are stringent to forbid profiting l'chatchila everywhere, likewise forbidden for donkey to bring chametz. Know: even for this view, specifically when he rented explicitly to bring chametz; but if he rented unstipulated for time and brought chametz, permitted — for if he carried nothing he would still pay wage, as we wrote above regarding oven.
mishnah-berurah/7:ג: (26) And some permit heating etc. — meaning: do not say this too is like wanting continued existence of chametz absorbed in vessel walls for the vessel's sake [when using it he wants it whole, and thereby like wanting chametz absorbed — for one cannot be without the other]; we do not say so for absorbed chametz not b'ein.
mishnah-berurah/7:ד: (27) And to wash in them — or to wash the head, for he benefits only from the vessel, not from chametz absorbed though it exudes into the water. Acharonim wrote: specifically vessels designated for washing and laundering not usually used for eating; but vessels sometimes used for eating and drinking must be stored modestly and not used even for washing — decree lest used for eating. Nevertheless temporary use — no stringency; explained later siman 451.
mishnah-berurah/7:ה: (28) And such is the custom — regarding selling chametz vessels to a non-Jew on Pesach, some permit, also for the reason above — he benefits only from the vessel body, not absorption [unless the non-Jew pays more because of absorption and there is difference — then he benefits from chametz]; some forbid. Acharonim wrote: a Jew holds an estate from a lord with a brewery house where they make beer called maltz; custom is whoever needs beer makes it in that house and the Jew takes rent; if he lets non-Jews make beer on Pesach, he wants chametz's continued existence because of vessels in the maltz [if maltz spills the cauldron cracks on the fire]; and when he receives rent he profits from issurei hana'ah; further, since custom is always to give a measure of maltz as wage not money — when the non-Jew makes beer the Jew already acquired the maltz measure, and even if given after Pesach forbidden — chametz of a Jew over which Passover passed. They wrote he should sell his right in the maltz to a non-Jew or rent for some weeks so Pesach days are absorbed and permitted; if he did not lease the maltz itself from the lord but only the measure-wages, sufficient to command brewers not to separate measures on Pesach but record they ground on Pesach and collect after — same for one holding mills on an estate.
turei-zahav/1:_: He should tell him before Pesach. So too Tur in the name of Avi HaEzri; and Beit Yosef wrote in Hagahot Maimoniyot and Mordechai regarding a Jew who bought the priests' allotment — he takes after Pesach what was withheld on Pesach; it implies no need to stipulate thus initially. The reason: here there is no prohibition but a fine for bal yera'eh, and here fining does not apply; he ruled to be stringent. It appears there is a difference in timing of the condition: in this law where he receives interest every week, each week is a separate debt — if he wants he can remove his money each week; when the Jew stipulates at week's start it is like a gift from the outset, unless he fixed interest once and cannot remove until the set time — then stipulation before Pesach does not help; learn from siman 245 regarding partnership with a non-Jew for Shabbat. Likewise here: since the Jew already acquired the loaf of the week of Pesach, what does stipulation help to remove himself — like selling chametz before Pesach he had on Pesach; not so if he stipulated initially the Jew did not acquire that loaf at all. Therefore one who buys the priests' allotment at once for a fixed term must stipulate at acquisition time for the reason mentioned, not later before Pesach; if he did not stipulate initially, his remedy is to void the transaction and stipulate then, as for Shabbat there. In a partnership oven with a non-Jew written afterwards — stipulation before Pesach helps there too: since half the oven is the Jew's he can always tell the non-Jew he does not want to participate on Pesach except on condition the non-Jew give him money for his share — this helps well in my humble opinion.
turei-zahav/2:_: He told him before Pesach etc. The rabbi's understanding here was hidden from me — "take yours for Pesach" etc., siman 443 — he benefits from Pesach chametz in what he takes for the week after Pesach, all the wage even the non-Jew's share because the non-Jew takes his share in the week of Pesach. Granted for Shabbat in siman 245 stipulation helps initially, at partnership formation — then the Jew never had a share that Shabbat, as Rashi explained there brought in Beit Yosef; not so here where they stipulated before Pesach and the non-Jew already has a share every week and the Jew a share every week — there is value to the Jew's chametz on Pesach; and even though they wrote nearby stipulation helps even before Pesach, that is so he can tell the non-Jew he will not give his share for work on Pesach unless he receives money — not chametz; then even if chametz given afterwards it is money substitutes. But here inapplicable — he stipulates he will in any event take chametz after Pesach for his Pesach share in what he already acquired at partnership start — what does stipulation help. In Tur in the name of Rashi: question why tell the non-Jew "take yours for Pesach and I afterwards"; answer: stipulate before Pesach and take money from that week. It appears "and take money" does not mean forbidden to receive chametz afterwards only money, but: stipulate before Pesach to take money; and as written in the seif before this, afterwards he may take even chametz. In the case Shulchan Aruch wrote it is wondrous — he changed from Rashi and Hagahot Maimoniyot Beit Yosef brings in something not permitted apparently; in Hagahot Maimoniyot Beit Yosef brings: but for Pesach permitted to stipulate before Pesach and take money of that week; and do not say regarding Jew etc.; but here since he takes money first, permitted (end). Beit Yosef wrote Mordechai did not mention needing to take money that week before Pesach etc.; truly Hagahot Maimoniyot seems not to require taking money first specifically, for they did not initially mention taking money before Pesach; and so responsum of Rashi and "further" chametz may be taken after Pesach as in previous seif — Avi HaEzri's words in Tur. Rather "from the start" means l'chatchila, referring to what follows "permitted" — since he takes money, even l'chatchila permitted; not as next seif that only if already received (in my humble opinion).
turei-zahav/3:_: Even money forbidden etc. In Tur after responsum 200, i.e. seif 3: Rashba wrote: an incident came before me — a Jew had an oven and a non-Jew baked chametz on Pesach; the baker, the Jew's treasurer, brought loaves after Pesach from oven-rent and I forbade receiving them — not only chametz forbidden because the Jew acquired through oven praise and it is the Jew's chametz, but even money forbidden as wage, profiting from issurei hana'ah, since chametz on Pesach is forbidden in benefit, even a non-Jew's chametz forbidden to benefit on Pesach (end). Apparently Tur and Rashba imply dispute with Rashi — Rashba forbids money Rashi permitted; that is not so — Rashi permitted because of stipulation before Pesach; for Rashba stipulation does not apply, loaves baked on Pesach were actually the Jew's — forbidden l'chatchila even money for them. The main dispute is as Beit Yosef in Rivash: some say do not rent one's animal to a non-Jew to bring chametz, holding a non-Jew's chametz forbidden in benefit; some rent and a non-Jew's chametz permitted in benefit — therefore since Rashi permitted taking money though coming from non-Jew's chametz, he holds like those who permit a non-Jew's chametz in benefit; Rashba wrote explicitly like those who forbid even a non-Jew's. Great wonder on Shulchan Aruch bringing Rashi in previous seif and Rashba here — for Rashba no remedy for a Jew's oven even in partnership with a non-Jew unless they stipulated at oven purchase that the Pesach week belongs to the non-Jew, like siman 245. On what Rashba wrote the Jew acquired loaves the treasurer brought after Pesach and forbidden — why not say here too he is pleased to acquire, not because of prohibition, as siman 448 regarding a non-Jew bringing chametz on yom tov the Jew can later say so and it is permitted — different there, no proof he wants acquisition on yom tov. Certainly here he is not pleased with the prohibition — unlike here chametz from today's act baking in his oven today when he gives the oven to bake today; certainly he is pleased — simple in my humble opinion; and see end of this siman.
turei-zahav/4:_: There are those who permit. This is Tosafot's view bringing proof from what we learn: he hired him for another work, even though he told him pass me yayin nesech barrels — permitted. One may say this case is different — there it is not proven he wants yayin nesech transfer, for many other works; not so for an oven — the non-Jew will certainly bake only chametz — as if rented explicitly for chametz. Further great difficulty, for it is written siman 256 seif 3: but it does not help if he stipulates with the non-Jew that his animal rest on Shabbat, for the non-Jew is not trusted — all the more here he will certainly bake chametz; requires further study.
turei-zahav/5:_: A house to dwell. But if specified to place chametz inside, forbidden on Pesach or erev Pesach; but more not so, Beit Yosef.
turei-zahav/6:_: Forbidden to rent etc. Tur's reason: wanting continued existence of chametz so the vessel not crack; and further since the vessel itself is forbidden in benefit, forbidden to rent l'chatchila. Do not say what the Tosefta teaches: one may rent one's donkey to a non-Jew for chametz — there the donkey is not forbidden but here the vessel is forbidden; this seems Rashba's view nearby, but Rashi's view we mentioned — for partnership oven permitted to rent when taking money — we could permit here too, but Tur's conclusion seems like Rashba. After the rules of this siman, proper to examine what is practiced in Russia and Volhynia: Jews rent an estate from the lord with cauldrons and mills; they take a measure of maltz from everyone who grinds maltz; maltz is full chametz punishable by karet — what to do on the week of Pesach. And a question: he wrote one should do through sale or giving to a non-Jew as siman 441; in my humble opinion there is doubt: one, sale does not apply to something not yet in existence, as Bava Metzia chapter 1 — "what my trap will bring, sell to you" — he said nothing; two, they permitted sale only when eating is permitted — "for me sale is like eating," as Mishnah: every hour eating is permitted, selling is permitted; so for chametz coming when eating forbidden, no proof sale is permitted — sale applies only until chametz exists, then eating forbidden. Further difficulty: do we have only one Pesach a year — we have more than fifty Pesachs, all Shabbats as Hillel the Elder said in chapter Elu Devarim regarding Pesach slaughter on Shabbat; we have more than two hundred Pesachs when Shabbat is overridden. We too say so here — how permit taking Shabbat wage on Shabbat, what the mill grinds on Shabbat — a measure for it — Shabbat wage clearly forbidden as explained in many places; we leave no permission for estate-holders and never heard Sages objected. Permission in my humble opinion like Yoreh De'ah siman 317 regarding raising lord's pigs — all belongs to the lord but the Jew takes from him; similar to buying priests' allotment at start of this siman — for views permitting even without stipulation, permitted to take the lord's allotment though not stipulated with anyone; and as we hold there stipulation required, here too for weekly interest mentioned above. For mills there is no fixed amount how much they grind; initially when buying he enters doubt whether they grind — then he takes each grinding automatically; each measure from the grinder is a new acquisition, as buying then from the lord — initial acquisition did not take effect until purchase existed, unclear at acquisition time; properly called non-Jew's chametz over which Passover passed when the Jew takes after Pesach; likewise after each Shabbat as intended initially — no fine applies, for R' Shimon fined only for bal yera'eh not applicable to the Jew on Pesach and Shabbat days. On Pesach itself the Jew acquired chametz after it came to existence — the Jew cannot say he is not pleased to acquire then, unlike siman 448; and though we wrote seif 4 in Rashba regarding oven praise — do not apply siman 448 there, different — oven is his and he willingly gives to bake that day, certainly pleased; not so mills belonging to the whole city, estate-holder cannot protest the non-Jew grinding that day — properly he can say he is not pleased to acquire at prohibition time since he can come after Pesach; certainly times mills are free from maltz grinding and whoever needs grinds also after Pesach — all applies to the lord's mills and Jew renting from him; but a Jew with his own mills certainly cannot give to grind on Shabbats and Pesach — like Rashba we mentioned: since he can protest and do as he wishes, no remedy except sell to a non-Jew for the year or half-year with Shabbat and Pesach absorbed between; unlike lord's mills — even though Jew already paid, sale did not take effect until it comes, since doubt at sale time what will come (in my humble opinion) to learn full permission; one who wants to be stringent should stipulate on Pesach that whoever wants to grind maltz gives a measure from other grain without chametz — then if maltz given after Pesach it is substitute for other grain, permitted as above.
turei-zahav/7:_: And to wash in them. Because he does not benefit from the absorption; and see siman 461.
